topics.title: Linear equations and equivalent expressions
topics.formula: a(x + b) = ax + ab; ax + b = c → x = (c − b)/a, a ≠ 0
topics.explain: Distribute, combine like terms, and perform the same operation on both sides. In a word problem, define the variable and translate the relationship before calculating.
topics.watch: A minus before parentheses changes every sign. Do not divide by an expression that may be zero without considering that case.

topics.title: Number of solutions and unknown constants
topics.formula: ax + b = cx + d → (a − c)x = d − b
topics.explain: If a ≠ c, there is one solution. If a = c and b = d, every real x works. If a = c and b ≠ d, there is no solution. Use these conditions to find an unknown parameter.
topics.example: 2x + 3 = 2x + 5 gives 3 = 5: no solution. For kx + 3 = 2x + 3 to have infinitely many solutions, k = 2.
topics.watch: An identity is true for every allowed input; a contradiction is true for none.

topics.title: Rearranging formulas
topics.formula: A = bh/2 → h = 2A/b, b ≠ 0
topics.explain: Treat all other letters as constants while isolating the requested quantity. Keep grouped sums together.
topics.watch: Dividing by a sum means dividing by the entire sum, not just one term.

topics.title: Slope and linear functions
topics.formula: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); y = mx + b; y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
topics.explain: Slope is output change per input unit; b is the output when x = 0. Point-slope form constructs a line from one point and its slope. A constant first difference for equally spaced x-values indicates a linear model.
topics.example: Through (2, 5) and (6, 13), m = 8/4 = 2. Then 5 = 2(2) + b gives b = 1.
topics.watch: A vertical line x = c has undefined slope; a horizontal line y = c has slope 0. A context may exclude x = 0 even when b exists algebraically.

topics.title: Intercepts, parallel and perpendicular lines
topics.formula: x-intercept: set y = 0; y-intercept: set x = 0; perpendicular nonvertical slopes: m₁m₂ = −1
topics.explain: Parallel distinct nonvertical lines have equal slopes and different intercepts. Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals; horizontal and vertical lines form the special case.
topics.example: For 2x + 3y = 12, intercepts are (6, 0) and (0, 4). Its slope is −2/3, so a perpendicular line has slope 3/2.
topics.watch: An intercept is a point; the x- or y-coordinate alone is often what the question asks for.

topics.title: Systems of two linear equations
topics.formula: Solve by substitution or elimination; graph intersections satisfy both equations
topics.explain: Multiply equations to cancel a variable, or isolate one variable and substitute. One intersection means one solution; parallel distinct lines mean none; identical lines mean infinitely many.
topics.example: x + y = 7 and 2x − y = 2 add to 3x = 9, so (x, y) = (3, 4).
topics.watch: When multiplying an equation, multiply every term, including the constant. Check both original equations.

topics.title: Inequalities and solution regions
topics.formula: If a < b and c < 0, then ac > bc
topics.explain: Reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. In two variables, graph the boundary and test a point; a system uses the overlap of the regions.
topics.example: −2x + 3 > 11 → −2x > 8 → x < −4. For y ≤ 2x + 1, include the boundary and shade below it.
topics.watch: Strict inequalities use a dashed boundary; ≤ and ≥ include it. An “and” statement needs both conditions; “or” needs at least one.

topics.title: Linear modeling and units
topics.formula: total cost = fixed cost + (cost per item)(number of items)
topics.explain: Define quantities with units. A coefficient is a rate; a constant is an initial or fixed amount. Tables, graphs, and equations can describe the same relationship.
topics.example: A rental costs $15 plus $4 per hour: C = 15 + 4h. A $35 budget gives h ≤ 5.
topics.watch: Do not reverse input and output units. A maximum budget or capacity usually creates an inequality.

topics.title: Exponent laws and scientific notation
topics.formula: aᵐaⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a⁰ = 1
topics.explain: These rules simplify products, quotients, and powers. Negative and zero exponent rules require a nonzero base. Scientific notation is c × 10ⁿ, with 1 ≤ |c| < 10.
topics.watch: Exponents do not distribute across addition: (x + y)² is not x² + y².

topics.title: Radicals and rational exponents
topics.explain: For positive a, rational exponent rules work directly. Real even roots require a nonnegative radicand; odd roots allow negatives. Factor perfect squares to simplify radicals.
topics.watch: The square-root symbol means the nonnegative root. The equation x² = 9 has two solutions, but √9 = 3.

topics.title: Polynomial operations and factoring
topics.formula: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); (a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b²
topics.explain: Combine only like powers; distribute all terms when multiplying. Factor out a greatest common factor first. In a monic quadratic x² + bx + c, find numbers with sum b and product c.
topics.watch: Cancel common factors, not terms separated by plus or minus signs.

topics.title: Quadratic equations and the quadratic formula
topics.explain: Use factoring, completing the square, or the formula. The zero-product rule says a product is zero only when at least one factor is zero.
topics.watch: Set the equation equal to zero before applying the formula. The denominator 2a applies to the whole numerator.

topics.title: Discriminant and root relationships
topics.formula: D = b² − 4ac; r₁ + r₂ = −b/a; r₁r₂ = c/a
topics.explain: D > 0 gives two distinct real roots, D = 0 one repeated real root, and D < 0 no real roots. Root sum and product follow by expanding a(x − r₁)(x − r₂).
topics.example: For x² + 6x + k = 0 to have exactly one real solution, 36 − 4k = 0, so k = 9.
topics.watch: “One real solution” counts the repeated root once. Root relationships require standard form with nonzero a.

topics.title: Quadratic graphs and completing the square
topics.formula: y = a(x − h)² + k; h = −b/(2a); k = f(h)
topics.explain: The vertex is (h, k). If a > 0, k is the minimum; if a < 0, it is the maximum. In factored form a(x − r₁)(x − r₂), the roots are visible.
topics.example: x² − 6x + 11 = (x − 3)² + 2, so the vertex is (3, 2) and the minimum is 2.
topics.watch: The vertex input is h, not −h. A contextual domain can make an endpoint the relevant maximum or minimum instead.

topics.title: Functions, notation, domain and range
topics.formula: f(a) means the output at input a; average rate = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a)
topics.explain: Substitute into the entire rule. Domain is the set of allowed inputs; range is the set of resulting outputs. Read zeros, intercepts, extrema, and intervals of increase from a graph.
topics.example: If f(x) = 2x² − 1, then f(3) = 17. For g(x) = √(x − 4), real inputs satisfy x ≥ 4 and outputs satisfy g(x) ≥ 0.
topics.watch: f(x) is not multiplication by f. A graph may be restricted by the real-world context.

topics.title: Function transformations
topics.formula: g(x) = a f(x − h) + k
topics.explain: h shifts the graph right; k shifts it up. A negative a reflects across the x-axis; |a| scales vertical distances. Replacing x by −x reflects across the y-axis.
topics.example: g(x) = −2(x − 3)² + 5 has vertex (3, 5), opens downward, and has a vertical scale factor 2.
topics.watch: Inside changes act in the opposite direction: f(x + 3) shifts left 3. f(2x) compresses horizontal distances by 1/2.

topics.title: Exponential growth and decay
topics.formula: y = A(1 + r)ᵗ; y = A(1 − r)ᵗ; y = A b^(t/k)
topics.explain: A is the initial quantity; r is a decimal rate per period. In the last form, b is the multiplier every k time units. Equal input increments produce a constant output ratio.
topics.example: A population of 500 grows 8% yearly: P = 500(1.08)ᵗ. After 2 years, P = 583.2. Doubling every 3 years uses A × 2^(t/3).
topics.watch: Match the period to the time unit. A multiplier 1.08 is 8% growth, not 108% growth. Linear change adds a fixed amount; exponential change multiplies.

topics.title: Solving exponential equations
topics.formula: If bᵘ = bᵛ with b > 0 and b ≠ 1, then u = v
topics.explain: Rewrite both sides using a common positive base when possible. For a context, a graph can identify the time when an exponential model reaches a target.
topics.watch: Do not equate exponents when bases differ. Check whether the question asks for elapsed time, an exponent, or the quantity itself.

topics.title: Rational expressions and equations
topics.formula: a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/(bd), b,d ≠ 0
topics.explain: Record denominator restrictions before simplifying. Factor, use a common denominator, and multiply an equation by its least common denominator to clear fractions.
topics.watch: A canceled denominator still excludes its original zeros. Reject any candidate that makes an original denominator zero.

topics.title: Radical and absolute-value equations
topics.formula: √u = v requires u ≥ 0 and v ≥ 0; |u| = c gives u = ±c if c ≥ 0
topics.explain: Isolate a radical before squaring, then check in the original equation. Absolute value is distance from zero; |x − a| is distance from a.
topics.example: √(x + 2) = x gives x² − x − 2 = 0. Candidates 2 and −1 arise, but only 2 works. |2x − 3| = 5 gives x = 4 or −1.
topics.watch: Squaring can introduce false solutions. |u| cannot equal a negative number.

topics.title: Nonlinear systems
topics.formula: At an intersection, both equations hold
topics.explain: Use substitution to reduce a line-parabola or other nonlinear system to one equation. Solve for every allowed input, then recover the corresponding output.
topics.example: y = x² and y = x + 2 give x² − x − 2 = 0, so intersections are (2, 4) and (−1, 1).
topics.watch: A tangency gives one intersection. Do not report only x-values if ordered pairs are requested.

topics.title: Polynomial zeros and equivalent forms
topics.formula: P(r) = 0 ⇔ (x − r) is a factor of polynomial P(x)
topics.explain: Factored form reveals zeros. Standard form reveals coefficients and the constant term. Rewriting an identity lets you compare matching coefficients.
topics.example: If x² + kx + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4) for every x, expanding the right gives k = 7.
topics.watch: An equality for one particular x does not let you equate all coefficients. A repeated factor may touch the axis rather than cross it.

topics.title: Ratios, proportions and rates
topics.formula: a/b = c/d → ad = bc; distance = rate × time; y = kx
topics.explain: A ratio compares quantities; a unit rate compares one unit of input. Direct proportion means a constant ratio y/x. Keep quantities in the same order.
topics.example: A mixture has red:blue = 2:3 and total 40. There are 5 ratio parts, each worth 8, so red = 16 and blue = 24.
topics.watch: The fraction of red is 2/5, not 2/3. Average speed is total distance divided by total time, not usually the mean of speeds.

topics.title: Unit conversions and density
topics.formula: density = mass/volume; population density = population/area
topics.explain: Multiply by conversion factors arranged so unwanted units cancel. Square a length conversion for area and cube it for volume.
topics.example: 3 m² = 3 × 100² cm² = 30,000 cm². A 120 g object occupying 40 cm³ has density 3 g/cm³.
topics.watch: 1 m² is not 100 cm². Always include units in intermediate work.

topics.title: Percentages and percent change
topics.formula: part = whole × p/100; percent change = 100(new − old)/old
topics.explain: The reference amount is the denominator. Apply successive increases or decreases by multiplying their factors. Reverse a change by dividing by the factor.
topics.example: After a 20% discount, an item costs $64: original = 64/0.8 = $80. A 20% rise then a 20% fall multiplies by 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96.
topics.watch: Percent change is different from percentage-point change: 30% to 40% is 10 points, but a 33⅓% relative increase.

topics.title: Mean and weighted mean
topics.formula: mean = sum/n; weighted mean = Σ(weight × value)/Σweights
topics.explain: Use frequencies as weights. A combined mean must account for different group sizes. The total equals the mean multiplied by the number of observations.
topics.example: Ten scores averaging 80 and twenty averaging 95 combine to (10 × 80 + 20 × 95)/30 = 90.
topics.watch: A simple average of group means is valid only when their weights are equal.

topics.title: Median, quartiles and spread
topics.formula: range = maximum − minimum; IQR = Q₃ − Q₁
topics.explain: Sort values before finding the median. For an even count, average the two middle values. Quartiles describe the middle half; standard deviation describes spread around the mean. Compare distributions and outlier sensitivity.
topics.example: For 2, 3, 4, 5, 16, the median is 4, mean is 6, and range is 14. The large value raises the mean more than the median.
topics.watch: A box plot does not show every individual value or determine the exact mean. Use the given quartile convention when calculation is requested.

topics.title: Transforming data
topics.formula:
Add c: mean and median increase by c; spread stays the same
Multiply by k: mean multiplies by k; standard deviation multiplies by |k|
topics.explain: Adding a constant shifts all observations equally. Multiplying changes distances by the absolute scale factor. Range and IQR also scale by |k|.
topics.example: If every measurement increases by 10, its standard deviation is unchanged. If every measurement doubles, its standard deviation doubles.
topics.watch: Changing only one observation is not the same as shifting the whole data set. More spread means larger standard deviation, not necessarily a larger mean.

topics.title: Frequency tables, histograms and box plots
topics.formula: relative frequency = category count/total count
topics.explain: Read axes and whether entries represent counts, proportions, or percentages. Histograms group numerical values into intervals; a box plot shows a five-number summary.
topics.example: If 12 of 40 students fall in a category, its relative frequency is 0.30 = 30%.
topics.watch: A histogram interval does not reveal each exact value. Do not infer exact individual scores or means from grouped values without sufficient information.

topics.title: Scatterplots, models and residuals
topics.formula: linear prediction: ŷ = mx + b; residual = observed y − predicted ŷ
topics.explain: Interpret direction, strength, and form of association. Choose a linear, quadratic, or exponential model based on the pattern. A residual measures prediction error.
topics.example: A model predicts 70 while the observed value is 74, so the residual is +4: the point lies above the model.
topics.watch: Association alone does not prove causation. Predictions far outside the observed input range are less reliable.

topics.title: Probability and complements
topics.formula: P(A) = favorable/total (equally likely outcomes); P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
topics.explain: Probabilities range from 0 to 1. Use counts or proportions from tables. For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add. In general P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
topics.example: If 7 of 20 equally likely outcomes are favorable, P(A) = 7/20 and P(not A) = 13/20.
topics.watch: Do not count overlapping outcomes twice. “Or” normally includes outcomes in both events.

topics.title: Conditional probability and independence
topics.formula: P(A given B) = P(A and B)/P(B), P(B) > 0
topics.explain: Restrict the sample space to B before calculating. Independent events satisfy P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). Sampling without replacement usually changes later probabilities.
topics.example: Among 30 students who take art, 12 also take music. P(music given art) = 12/30 = 0.4.
topics.watch: The denominator is the condition group, not the entire population. Mutually exclusive nonzero-probability events are not independent.

topics.title: Sampling, estimates and margin of error
topics.formula:
estimated count = sample proportion × population size
interval = estimate ± margin of error
topics.explain: A representative random sample supports estimates about its population. A margin of error describes sampling uncertainty; larger comparable random samples tend to reduce it.
topics.example: An estimate of 52% with a 4-point margin gives 48% to 56%. A sample proportion 0.30 predicts about 600 of 2,000 people.
topics.watch: A larger sample does not repair selection bias. A sample result is an estimate, not an exact population count; an interval is not a guarantee.

topics.title: Study design and evaluating claims
topics.formula:
Random sampling → population generalization
Random assignment → evidence for cause and effect in a well-designed experiment
topics.explain: Observational studies measure existing conditions; experiments assign treatments. Random assignment helps balance other factors between groups. Consider control groups, confounding, and the population actually sampled.
topics.example: Randomly assigning volunteers to two study methods can support a causal comparison for similar participants; recruiting only volunteers limits broad generalization.
topics.watch: Random selection and random assignment solve different problems. A correlation from observation alone does not establish causation.

topics.title: Lines, angles and polygons
topics.formula:
straight angle = 180°; full turn = 360°; triangle angles sum to 180°
interior-angle sum of an n-sided polygon = (n − 2)180°
topics.explain: Vertical angles are equal. With parallel lines, corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal; same-side interior angles sum to 180°. A triangle exterior angle equals the two remote interior angles combined.
topics.example: A triangle with angles 48° and 67° has third angle 65°. A regular hexagon has each interior angle 720°/6 = 120°.
topics.watch: Equal-looking angles are not enough: use stated parallel lines or marked relationships. Diagrams need not be to scale.

topics.title: Triangle similarity and congruence
topics.formula: similar lengths scale by k; areas by k²; volumes of similar solids by k³
topics.explain: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. AA proves similarity; SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS can prove triangle congruence.
topics.example: Similar triangles have corresponding sides 4 and 10, so k = 2.5. A side of 6 corresponds to 15; an area of 8 corresponds to 50.
topics.watch: Match corresponding vertices before writing a proportion. Equal areas do not imply congruent shapes.

topics.title: Triangle facts and the Pythagorean theorem
topics.formula: a² + b² = c² for a right triangle; |a − b| < c < a + b
topics.explain: c is the hypotenuse opposite the right angle. The triangle inequality limits any third side. Equal sides in an isosceles triangle face equal angles.
topics.example: A right triangle with legs 6 and 8 has hypotenuse √100 = 10. Sides 4 and 7 require the third side to be greater than 3 and less than 11.
topics.watch: The Pythagorean theorem applies only to right triangles. The hypotenuse is the longest side.

topics.title: Special right triangles
topics.explain: In the second ratio, x is opposite 30°, x√3 opposite 60°, and 2x is the hypotenuse. These relationships are available on the SAT reference sheet.
topics.example: If a 30°–60°–90° triangle has hypotenuse 12, its legs are 6 and 6√3.
topics.watch: Identify the angle opposite each side; do not assume x labels whichever side is given.

topics.title: Right-triangle trigonometry
topics.formula: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse; cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse; tan θ = opposite/adjacent
topics.explain: For an acute angle in a right triangle, label sides relative to that angle. Also sin θ = cos(90° − θ) and sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
topics.example: For a 3–4–5 triangle and the angle opposite side 3, sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5, and tan θ = 3/4.
topics.watch: Opposite and adjacent switch when the reference angle changes. Use degrees or radians consistently with the prompt.

topics.title: Area, perimeter and surface area
topics.formula:
rectangle: A = lw; triangle: A = bh/2; parallelogram: A = bh
trapezoid: A = (b₁ + b₂)h/2
topics.explain: Perimeter adds boundary lengths. Height is perpendicular to the base. For composite figures, add component areas or subtract holes. Surface area adds the areas of all exposed faces.
topics.example: A trapezoid with bases 6 and 10 and height 4 has area 32. A 2 × 3 × 4 box has surface area 2(6 + 8 + 12) = 52.
topics.watch: A slanted side is not necessarily a height. Area uses square units; perimeter uses length units.

topics.title: Circle area, circumference and angles
topics.formula: A = πr²; C = 2πr = πd; d = 2r
topics.explain: A central angle equals the measure of its intercepted arc in degrees. An inscribed angle is half the intercepted arc; an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.
topics.example: A circle of radius 5 has area 25π and circumference 10π. An inscribed angle intercepting an 80° arc is 40°.
topics.watch: Using diameter as radius makes the area four times too large. An arc length is a distance, not an angle measure.

topics.title: Arc length, sector area and radians
topics.formula:
s = (θ/360°)2πr; sector area = (θ/360°)πr²
s = rθ and sector area = r²θ/2 when θ is in radians; 180° = π radians
topics.explain: An arc and sector take the same fraction of the whole circle as their central angle. Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by π/180.
topics.example: A 60° sector of a radius-6 circle has arc length 2π and area 6π. The angle is π/3 radians.
topics.watch: The formulas s = rθ and A = r²θ/2 require radians, not degrees.

topics.title: Coordinate distance, midpoint and circles
topics.formula:
distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]
midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)
(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
topics.explain: A circle has center (h, k) and radius r. Complete the square in x and y to recover the center from expanded form. Distance comes from the Pythagorean theorem.
topics.example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y = 12 becomes (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25: center (3, −2), radius 5.
topics.watch: Read radius as the square root of the right-hand constant. Signs inside the squares are opposite the center coordinates.

topics.title: Volume of prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres
topics.formula:
prism: V = Bh; cylinder: V = πr²h; pyramid: V = Bh/3
cone: V = πr²h/3; sphere: V = 4πr³/3
topics.explain: B is base area and h is perpendicular height. A rectangular prism uses B = lw. Combine or subtract solid volumes when a shape has multiple components.
topics.example: A cylinder with radius 3 and height 10 has volume 90π. A cone with the same radius and height has volume 30π.
topics.watch: Volume uses cubic units. Doubling every dimension multiplies volume by 8, not 2. Do not use slant height for a cone’s volume.

topics.title: Translate, solve, interpret and check
topics.formula: Define → model → solve → check → answer the requested quantity
topics.explain: Write what each variable means. Convert units first, use the structure of the expression, and substitute your result back. Check positivity, integer constraints, denominator restrictions, and the context.
topics.example: If x is the number of packs but the question asks for total items and each pack has 12, the final answer is 12x, not x.
topics.watch: A mathematically valid root may be impossible as a negative length, a fractional number of people, or a time outside the model.

topics.title: Use graphs and a calculator strategically
topics.formula: Roots solve f(x) = 0; intersections solve f(x) = g(x)
topics.explain: A graphing calculator can check roots, intersections, vertices, tables, and fitted models. Use algebra for exact values and parameter relationships. Estimate first and choose a window that shows the relevant inputs.
topics.example: To solve x² = 2x + 3, graph both sides and find x = −1 and 3; substitution confirms them exactly.
topics.watch: A graph window can hide solutions. A rounded decimal near 1/3 is not proof of an exact fraction. Confirm the calculator’s angle mode for trigonometry.

topics.title: Reference sheet versus understanding
topics.formula: Know what each symbol means and when the relationship applies
topics.explain: The standard SAT reference information includes common circle, rectangle, triangle and solid-volume formulas, special right triangles, the Pythagorean theorem, and angle totals. Algebra, percent reasoning, statistics, and interpreting models still require understanding.
topics.example: If given a diameter, first halve it before using A = πr². If a triangle’s height is not stated, derive the perpendicular height before using A = bh/2.
topics.watch: This guide covers the core content domains, not every possible wording or problem. Pair review with official practice and explanation of your own mistakes.
